paragraphs.heading: Multiplying down to one
paragraphs.text: The factorial of a whole number n is written with an exclamation mark, as n!, and it is what you get when you multiply together every positive whole number from 1 up to n. Each value can also be found from the one before it, using the rule n! = n⋅(n − 1)!, so that 5! = 5⋅4! = 5⋅24 = 120. The numbers being multiplied are the factors that give the factorial its name.

paragraphs.heading: Counting arrangements
paragraphs.text: The most basic job of the factorial is counting permutations, the different orders in which n distinct objects can be lined up. The number of such orders is exactly n!, no more and no fewer. This was also the earliest use of factorials, and they turn up across combinatorics wherever a formula has to account for objects being put in different orders. A related count is of derangements, orders in which no object stays in its starting place; for n items their number is the whole number closest to n!/e.

paragraphs.heading: Why zero factorial is one
paragraphs.text: By convention the factorial of zero equals 1. The reason is that it is a product of no numbers at all, and such an empty product is taken to equal 1. It also fits counting: there is exactly one way to arrange zero objects, which is to do nothing. With this choice, the rule n! = n⋅(n − 1)! still works when n is 1, so a computer program that finds factorials step by step needs only zero as its starting case.

paragraphs.heading: An old idea in many places
paragraphs.text: Factorials were found in several ancient cultures. In India, an early account appears in the Anuyogadvāra-sūtra, a Jain text dated anywhere from 300 BCE to 400 CE. The Hebrew book Sefer Yetzirah, from the Talmudic period, lists factorials up to 7! as part of asking how many words can be built from the Hebrew alphabet. In 1150, Bhāskara II used them to count the ways the god Vishnu could hold four objects in his four hands.

paragraphs.heading: From bells to an exclamation mark
paragraphs.text: Western mathematicians took up factorials from the late 15th century. In 1494 Luca Pacioli worked them out up to 11! in a problem about seating people at a dining table. In 1677 Fabian Stedman applied them to change ringing, the musical art of ringing a set of tuned bells. The notation n! came from the French mathematician Christian Kramp in 1808.

paragraphs.heading: Fast growth and prime numbers
paragraphs.text: Factorials get large very fast, faster than exponential growth, and Stirling's approximation gives an accurate estimate of their size for large numbers. They also carry a link to prime numbers, since n! can be divided by every positive whole number up to n. From this it follows that the prime factors of n! ± 1 can be arbitrarily large, which leads to a proof that there are infinitely many primes.
